narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 55.6% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. At 27, it sits well below the average of 37 among students who were accepted, signaling weaker preparation in the eyes of the model. Your undergraduate GPA was the second most important factor and worked in your favor, pulling the prediction toward passing. A 3.8 GPA is notably stronger than the 3.23 average of accepted students, giving you a meaningful advantage there. Your third-year class ranking came in third. Placing in the fourth decile (compared to an average around the sixth decile for accepted students) modestly increased the predicted risk of failure.

Taken together, the lower LSAT score outweighed your strong GPA and contributed most to the rejection. 

What you should do next is clear: focus on raising your LSAT score through targeted preparation. A higher score on a retake would likely shift the model’s prediction enough to change the admissions outcome. Consider reapplying once you have improved that key area.
